A landlady is a woman who owns a property — such as a house, a flat, or a set of rooms — and allows other people to live in it in exchange for regular payments called rent. She owns the place; she does not live there as a tenant herself (though sometimes she does — more on that below). The people who pay her and live in her property are called her tenants.

Think of it this way: if you move into an apartment and a woman owns the building and collects your rent each month, she is your landlady.

1. A Woman Who Rents Out Property

This is the most common modern meaning. A landlady owns residential property — a house, a flat, a room, or even a piece of land — and rents it to others for income.

"She saved up for years, bought a small house, and became a landlady by renting it out to a young couple."

She may own just one property or many. Her main responsibilities typically include collecting rent, maintaining the property, and ensuring her tenants have a livable space.

2. A Woman Who Runs a Pub, Inn, or Boarding House

This is an older and more specifically British usage, though it is still alive today. A pub (a public house, i.e., a bar) or a traditional inn is often managed by a woman who holds the license to run the establishment. She is called the landlady of the pub or inn.

"The landlady of The Crown Inn greeted every regular customer by name."

In this sense, she may not necessarily own the building — she may rent it from a brewery or company — but she is the one who runs it, serves the drinks, and is in charge of the place. This usage is deeply rooted in British culture.

Similarly, a boarding house is a private home where the owner rents out rooms, often including meals. The woman who runs such a place is the landlady.
The Gender Point — Landlady vs. Landlord

The word "landlady" specifically refers to a woman. The masculine equivalent is landlord.

  • A man who owns property and rents it out → landlord
  • A woman who owns property and rents it out → landlady

In modern usage, "landlord" is increasingly used as a gender-neutral term for both men and women, the same way "actor" has largely replaced "actress" in professional contexts. However, "landlady" is still widely used and clearly understood whenever the owner/operator is a woman.
A Special Case: The Resident Landlady

Sometimes, a landlady lives in the same property that she rents out rooms from. For example, she might own a large house, live on the ground floor herself, and rent the upstairs rooms to others. In this case, the people renting from her are usually called lodgers (rather than tenants), and she is sometimes called a resident landlady.

The distinction matters in some countries legally, but in everyday speech, the word "landlady" covers both situations.

Understanding a word fully also means knowing the words around it:

  • Landlady — the woman who owns/runs the property
  • Landlord — the man who owns/runs the property
  • Tenant — a person who rents a home or flat from a landlord/landlady
  • Lodger — a person who rents a single room, often within the landlady's own home
  • Rent — the money a tenant or lodger pays the landlady, usually monthly
  • Lease / Tenancy agreement — the legal contract between the landlady and the tenant
  • Property — the building or land the landlady owns

Renting a flat:

"My landlady lives in another city, so she uses an agency to manage the property."

Living as a lodger:

"When he first moved to London, he rented a room from a kind landlady who cooked breakfast every morning."

Running a pub:

"The landlady pulled a fresh pint of beer and slid it across the counter."

Historical/literary use:

"Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson lived at 221B Baker Street, where their landlady, Mrs. Hudson, looked after them."

(Mrs. Hudson is arguably the most famous landlady in all of English literature.)

Plural use:

"Many landladies in the city raised their rents after the new transport line opened."

The word "landlady" is perfectly standard — it is neither slang nor overly formal. You can use it in casual conversation, in writing, in a legal discussion, or in literature without it sounding out of place.

It carries no inherently negative connotation, though in literature and fiction, the landlady character is sometimes portrayed as nosy, strict, or intimidating — this is a cultural stereotype, not something built into the word itself.
The plural of landlady is landladies (following the standard rule: drop the y, add ies).

A landlady is a woman who either (a) owns property and rents it out to tenants for income, or (b) owns or manages a pub, inn, or boarding house. The word is the female form of "landlord." It is a common, neutral, everyday word in English — especially in British English — and it captures a clear, specific role: the woman who holds authority over a rented space, whether that space is a flat, a room, or a pub.
